**Verdict: skim the tables, skip the prose — unless you're building a SKILL.md linter, in which case read it.**

**What it gives you**
- A component taxonomy for SKILL.md (13 higher-level / 44 lower-level), derived from qualitative coding of 238 real files.
- 26 named "skill smells," each the inverse of a community best practice, grouped into 11 categories (under-specified guidance, over-prescription, missing verification, context bloat, missing safeguards, security, style, output).
- An automated detector: 5 smells checked statically, 21 by an LLM judge. Weighted F1 0.78 on 53 hand-labeled files.
- Evolution data: 1,295 commits over 142 skills, Oct 2025 – Jun 2026. Smells rarely get removed once introduced.

**Headline numbers**
- >99% of skills carry at least one smell; 10.5 on average; only 1 of 238 files is clean.
- Rationalization Loophole (nothing discourages the agent from skipping steps) hits 94%.
- Component coverage is thin past the top few: Task 74%, Introduction 64%, References 57%, then a fast drop to Output Format 24% and below.
- Only 7 of 13 component types have any community guidance at all.

**Why the findings are weak**
The "best practices" are folklore: top-50 web sources, filtered to 29, conflicts resolved by majority vote. Nothing links smells to worse agent behavior, so the paper establishes prevalence, not harm. The sample is popular public marketplace skills, which may not resemble internal ones. Detector accuracy rests on 53 labeled files and a single 4-bit quantized open model.

**If you're deciding**
Read it for the smell catalog and the judge prompt design (per-smell definition + one positive + one negative example, binary answer, thinking mode) — those are directly reusable as a rubric and a detector baseline to beat. Don't read it for evidence that any of this improves skill quality; that work hasn't been done.
